passages.t: Whom are you seeking? I am He
passages.happening:
After the prayer Jesus leads his friends out of the city, “across the Kidron Valley, where they entered a garden” (verse 1). Judas knows the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples (verse 2).

Judas comes with a band of soldiers and with officers sent by the chief priests and Pharisees, “carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons” (verse 3). Jesus does not hide. Knowing all that is coming, he steps forward and asks, “Whom are you seeking?” (verse 4). “Jesus of Nazareth,” they say. He answers, “I am He”, and they draw back and fall to the ground (verses 5-6).

He asks again, and then says, “So if you are looking for Me, let these men go” (verse 8). Simon Peter draws a sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant, whose name was Malchus (verse 10). Jesus stops him: “Put your sword back in its sheath!” Then he asks, “Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The Kidron is the valley that runs down the east side of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives. The other Gospels name the garden Gethsemane (Mark 14:32). John does not tell of Jesus' anguished prayer there. In John he has just prayed, and now he walks out to meet what is coming.

Look at who comes. John's word for the ‘band of soldiers’ is speira, the usual word for a Roman cohort, a unit of several hundred men, and in verse 12 he names its commander with the Greek word for a Roman tribune. Most scholars think a detachment, not the whole unit, came with the temple officers. Either way, John is saying that Rome and the temple's rulers acted together from the first moment.

Then Jesus says, ‘I am He’. In Greek it is two words, egō eimi, ‘I am’. It can be an ordinary way of saying ‘That's me’. But John has used the same words for Jesus' greatest claims, “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58). Here armed men fall to the ground at them. John wants the reader to hear more than a man giving his name.

And notice what Jesus does with his authority. He uses it to protect his friends: ‘let these men go’. John says this fulfilled his own words in the prayer: ‘I have not lost one of those You have given Me’ (verse 9).

Only John names Peter as the one with the sword, and Malchus as the servant. Luke adds that Jesus touched the man's ear and healed him (Luke 22:51).
passages.ot:
When King David fled from Jerusalem, betrayed by his own son and his trusted adviser, “the king crossed the Kidron Valley” and went up the Mount of Olives, weeping (2 Samuel 15:23, 15:30). A thousand years later David's greater son crosses the same valley, betrayed by a friend. Readers have long noticed the echo, though John does not point it out.

God spoke through Isaiah, “so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He” (Isaiah 43:10). A psalm says of the righteous man's attackers, “my enemies and foes stumbled and fell” (Psalm 27:2).

The cup Jesus will drink is a prophets' picture of suffering and of God's judgment, as when Jerusalem is said to have drunk “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17). Jesus takes it from his Father's hand.
passages.hard:
Why did they fall to the ground? John does not explain, and readers have answered in different ways. Many think John shows a flash of Jesus' divine majesty: the men who came to take him are thrown back by his word, so that the reader knows he is not taken against his will. Others think startled men in the dark simply stumbled back from a man who walked straight toward them. John's point is the same in either reading. As Jesus said earlier, “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (10:18).

And the sword? Peter acts out of love and courage, and Jesus stops him. Jesus does not want to be defended this way. Matthew records his words, “all who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). Christians have argued for centuries about whether force is ever right, and the note on Matthew 26 sets out those views. What this scene settles is narrower and plain: Jesus' own cause is not to be advanced by a sword.
passages.asks: Jesus walked out to meet the men who came for him, and he used his last free moment to protect his friends. Ask what it means that he was not trapped, but chose this. And ask where you, like Peter, have tried to fight for Jesus in a way he never asked of you. The cup was his to drink. He did not need Peter's sword. He needed Peter to trust him.

passages.t: To Annas, and a fire in the courtyard
passages.happening:
The soldiers, their commander and “the officers of the Jews”, the temple police sent by the chief priests, arrest Jesus and tie him up (verse 12). They take him first to Annas, “the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year” (verse 13). John reminds the reader that Caiaphas was the one who had said it would be better for one man to die for the people (verse 14).

Simon Peter and “another disciple” follow. That disciple is known to the high priest, so he goes into the courtyard and then speaks to the doorkeeper and brings Peter in (verses 15-16).

The servant girl at the door asks Peter, “Aren't you also one of this man's disciples?” He answers, “I am not” (verse 17). It is cold. The servants and officers have made a charcoal fire, and Peter stands with them, warming himself (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Only John tells of Jesus being taken to Annas first. Annas had been high priest himself, appointed in AD 6 and removed by the Roman governor about AD 15. But his family kept the office. Josephus says that five of his sons became high priest, which had never happened to anyone else, and Caiaphas was his son-in-law. So Annas still held great power, with or without the title. Luke pairs the two men in the same way (Luke 3:2).

When John writes ‘the Jews’ in this chapter, he means, here and most often, the temple authorities and their officers. ‘The officers of the Jews’ are the temple police who serve the chief priests. Jesus himself, Peter, the other disciple and the servant girl are all Jews too. The book page explains this in ‘The Jews in John’.

Who is the ‘other disciple’? John does not say. Many readers think he is the disciple whom Jesus loved. As the book page says, if he is the disciple ‘known to the high priest’, that would fit the view that the beloved disciple was a follower from Jerusalem. Others think the phrase points elsewhere. No one can be sure.

Notice the fire. John's word is anthrakia, a fire of charcoal. It appears only twice in the New Testament: here, where Peter denies Jesus beside it, and in John 21:9, where the risen Jesus has a charcoal fire waiting on the shore.
passages.ot: Caiaphas had said more than he knew: “it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish” (11:50). John said he spoke as a prophet without meaning to (11:51). Isaiah had pictured the servant of the LORD who would die for others: “He was led like a lamb to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7). Caiaphas meant a political bargain. God meant a sacrifice.
passages.hard:
Why does John tell Peter's denial in two pieces, with the questioning of Jesus in between? Mark and Matthew tell the three denials together. John cuts back and forth. Inside, Jesus stands before the high priest and says, in effect, ‘I have nothing to hide.’ Outside, Peter stands by the fire and says, ‘I am not.’ Jesus has just said ‘I am He’ to armed men. Peter says ‘I am not’ to a servant girl.

That contrast is not there to shame Peter. It is there so that the reader sees how far a sincere follower can fall in one night, and how steady Jesus stays. The Mark 14 note says it plainly: a person can mean a promise with all their heart and still break it a few hours later. Sincerity is not the same as strength.
passages.asks: Peter got close enough to see what happened, and then he could not admit who he was. Ask where you have stayed near Jesus but kept quiet about him, warming yourself at someone else's fire. And remember where this story is going. There will be another charcoal fire, on a beach, and the same man will be asked a different question.

passages.t: I have spoken openly, and Peter denies again
passages.happening:
Inside, the high priest questions Jesus “about His disciples and His teaching” (verse 19). Jesus answers, “I have spoken openly to the world,” and goes on, “I always taught in the synagogues and at the temple, where all the Jews come together. I said nothing in secret” (verse 20). If they want to know what he taught, they should ask the people who heard him (verse 21).

One of the officers slaps him in the face: “Is this how You answer the high priest?” (verse 22). Jesus replies, “If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?” (verse 23). Annas sends him, still bound, to Caiaphas (verse 24).

Outside, Peter is still warming himself. They ask again, and again he says, “I am not” (verse 25). Then a relative of Malchus asks, “Didn't I see you with Him in the garden?” (verse 26). Peter denies it once more, “and immediately a rooster crowed” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
This is not a formal trial. It is a questioning in the night by the most powerful man in the priestly family. Annas asks about Jesus' disciples and teaching, perhaps looking for a secret movement, a plot against Rome or the temple.

Jesus' answer is a fair one. In a court of that time, as in ours, a charge was to be proved by witnesses. The law of Moses required two or three (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus taught in public, in synagogues and in the temple courts, ‘where all the Jews come together’; here the phrase simply means the Jewish people gathered for worship, with no hostility at all. So, he says, ask the witnesses.

Later Jewish law, written down in the Mishnah around AD 200, set out careful rules for capital trials. The note on Mark 14 explains that historians differ on how far those rules were followed in Jesus' day, and some think they describe a later ideal. These notes do not judge the hearing by them.

John's account of Peter does not say he cursed, as Mark does (Mark 14:71). Nor does it tell of Peter weeping. It ends on the rooster, the sound Jesus had foretold (13:38), and leaves Peter standing there.
passages.ot:
The law said, “You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28). The officer thinks Jesus has broken it. But Jesus has said nothing disrespectful. He has asked for justice.

Isaiah's servant says, “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard” (Isaiah 50:6). Jesus does not hit back, but he does not keep silent either. He names the injustice calmly: ‘why did you strike Me?’
passages.hard:
Jesus had taught, “If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). Here he is struck and asks why. Is that a contradiction? Many readers think not. Jesus does not strike back or curse. But turning the other cheek never meant pretending that wrong is right. He speaks the truth to the man who hit him, without revenge. A Christian can refuse to hit back and still say plainly, ‘That was wrong.’

The note on Matthew 5 points to this very verse. Jesus speaks of refusing revenge, not of accepting abuse. Seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus. If you are being harmed, tell someone you trust and get help.
passages.asks: Jesus had nothing to hide. Everything he taught, he taught in the open. Ask whether your faith could stand being looked at in daylight, or whether there are parts you keep in the dark. And notice the rooster. It was not Peter's punishment. It was a reminder that Jesus had known all along, and had not let go of him.

passages.happening:
Early in the morning they lead Jesus from Caiaphas to the Praetorium, the Roman governor's headquarters. The leaders who brought him do not go in, “to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover” (verse 28).

So Pilate comes out to them: “What accusation are you bringing against this man?” (verse 29). They answer, “If He were not a criminal,” and add that they would not have handed him over otherwise (verse 30). Pilate tells them to judge him by their own law. They reply, “We are not permitted to execute anyone” (verse 31).

John adds that this happened to fulfill what Jesus had said about the kind of death he would die (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Praetorium is a Latin word for a commander's headquarters. In Jerusalem it meant the place where the governor stayed when he came up from Caesarea for the feasts. Scholars debate where that was. The old tradition places it at the Antonia fortress next to the temple. Many scholars now think it was Herod's former palace on the west side of the city.

Why would the leaders not go in? A house of Gentiles, people who were not Jews, was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean. Peter later says, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him” (Acts 10:28). Someone unclean could not eat the Passover until he was clean again. John lets the irony stand: they take great care over the feast while handing an innocent man to be killed.

Notice, too, John's timing. On this morning ‘the Passover’ has not yet been eaten. The note on Mark 14 explains that this is one of the places where John seems to place the Last Supper and the crucifixion a day earlier than Mark, and it sets out the answers Christians have given. No answer has won general agreement.

‘We are not permitted to execute anyone.’ The Mark 15 note explains this. Historians discuss how strict the limit was, since Jewish authorities did sometimes carry out killings, such as the stoning of Stephen. But crucifixion was a Roman punishment, carried out under a Roman governor's authority.

John's ‘the Jews’ in verses 28 and 31 are the chief priests and their officers who brought Jesus, as 19:6 will say outright, not the Jewish people.

A small piece of history sits on these verses. The oldest known scrap of any New Testament book is a small fragment of papyrus, kept in the John Rylands Library in Manchester and published in 1935. On one side it has words from John 18:31-33, and on the other from 18:37-38. Scholars date it to the 100s; many have said around 125, and some argue for later in that century.
passages.ot:
The law said that a man who was unclean could not keep the Passover on the set day (Numbers 9:6). The leaders are careful about that law.

Verse 32 points back to Jesus' own words: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself” (12:32), said “to indicate the kind of death He was going to die” (12:33). Stoning would not lift him up. A Roman cross would, as Moses lifted up the bronze snake in the wilderness (3:14, Numbers 21:8-9). The law of Moses also said that “anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul later saw in this that Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
passages.hard: Is John against the Jewish law here? No. The law about cleanness for the Passover was God's law, and Jesus kept the feasts. John's irony falls on particular leaders who used careful religion to cover an unjust act. Every religious person, Christians included, can do the same thing: keep the rules carefully while doing wrong. The warning is for the church as much as anyone.
passages.asks: The leaders would not step into a Gentile's house in case it spoiled their feast, and on the same morning they handed over an innocent man. Ask where you are careful about small things and careless about large ones. It is one of the oldest ways of being religious without being good.

passages.t: My kingdom is not of this world. What is truth?
passages.happening:
Pilate goes back inside, calls Jesus, and asks, “Are You the King of the Jews?” (verse 33). Jesus asks whether he says this on his own or because others told him (verse 34). “Am I a Jew?” Pilate replies. “Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?” (verse 35).

Jesus answers, “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews. But now My kingdom is not of this realm” (verse 36).

“Then You are a king!” Pilate says. Jesus answers, “You say that I am a king,” and then, “For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice” (verse 37).

“What is truth?” Pilate asks (verse 38). Without waiting, he goes out and tells the crowd, “I find no basis for a charge against Him.”
passages.hearers:
To a Roman governor, ‘King of the Jews’ meant one thing: a rebel. Rome named the kings in its provinces. A man who claimed to be king without Rome's leave was a threat to be crushed. That is why the charge matters.

Jesus' answer turns on a small Greek word. His kingdom is not ek tou kosmou toutou, not ‘from this world’. He is speaking about where his kingdom comes from and what kind it is, not about where it is. It does not come from the world's power, and so it does not grow the world's way. If it did, his followers would be fighting. They are not. Peter's sword is back in its sheath.

‘Truth’ in John is not only correct information. It is what is real about God, made known in Jesus, who said, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life’ (14:6). Pilate stands face to face with the truth and asks what it is.

Pilate's question has echoed ever since. In 1625 the English writer Francis Bacon began his essay ‘Of Truth’ with the line, ‘What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.’ John does not say whether Pilate was jesting, weary or bitter. He only says that Pilate walked out without waiting.

‘Your own people and chief priests handed You over’: in verse 36 ‘the Jews’ who arrested Jesus are these same authorities and their officers. Jesus is a Jew speaking of the leaders of his own nation, and his disciples, who would have fought for him, were Jews too.
passages.ot:
Daniel saw one like a son of man given a kingdom from God: “His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 7:14). That kingdom comes from God, not from the beasts of earthly empire in the same vision.

Zechariah's king comes “humble and riding on a donkey”, and God says, “the bow of war will be broken. Then He will proclaim peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:9-10). Jesus rode into Jerusalem that way a few days before (12:14-15). His kingdom was always meant to be a kingdom of peace.
passages.hard:
‘My kingdom is not of this world’ has been misused in two opposite ways, and both should be named plainly.

The first misuse says that because Jesus' kingdom is not of this world, his followers should leave the world alone: faith is a private matter for the soul, and justice, the poor and public life are none of its business. But Jesus does not say his kingdom is absent from this world. He says it does not come from it. The same Jesus taught his followers to pray, ‘Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven’ (Matthew 6:10), and he sent them into the world (17:18).

The second misuse goes the other way. It treats Jesus' kingship as a warrant to make the state Christian, to win his kingdom with the tools of government, law or force. But Jesus says that if his kingdom were that kind, his servants would fight, and they do not. Christians in many centuries have tried to bring in his kingdom by the sword or the ballot, and they have often harmed both the church and their neighbors.

Christians hold different views about how faith should shape public life, and these notes take no party's side. This verse rules out only the two errors: that the kingdom has nothing to say to the world, and that it can be built with the world's power.
passages.asks: Pilate had the truth standing in front of him, and he walked out without waiting for an answer. Ask whether you ask big questions in order to hear an answer, or in order to avoid one. And ask what it would mean to belong to a kingdom that does not fight the world's way: whose King answers force with truth.

passages.happening:
Pilate reminds the crowd of a custom. Each Passover he releases one prisoner to them. “So then, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” (verse 39).

“Not this man,” they shout, “but Barabbas!” John adds one line: “(Now Barabbas was an insurrectionist.)” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The other Gospels tell this scene at more length. Mark says Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising (Mark 15:7). The note on Mark 15 explains what is known of the Passover release: it is known only from the Gospels, and historians debate it. Some think it a literary creation; others note festival pardons elsewhere.

John's word for Barabbas is lēstēs. It can mean a robber, but it was often used of armed rebels, the bandits of the hills who fought Rome. So the crowd is offered a choice between two men called dangerous to Rome. One fought with a sword. The other told Pilate a moment ago that his servants would not fight.

Many readers have noticed the name too. Barabbas means ‘son of the father’ in Aramaic. The true Son of the Father is condemned, and a man who bears that name goes free.

In John's account it is ‘they’ who shout: the chief priests and their officers, as 19:6 will say outright. John does not describe a whole nation. He describes the people in one courtyard on one morning.
passages.ot: Isaiah's servant was “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). Here Jesus is counted lower than a known rebel. And Isaiah says of the servant that “the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). Barabbas walks free because Jesus takes his place.
passages.hard: Was the choice of Barabbas a choice by the Jewish people? No, and this passage has been misused to say so. The full answer belongs to the next chapter, where John tells of the chief priests' cry, and the note on 19:13-16 faces it there. For now, notice what John actually says: a particular group in one place on one morning, stirred by particular leaders, before a Roman governor who could have released Jesus and did not.
passages.asks: Barabbas is the only man in the story who can say, plainly and literally, ‘Jesus died in my place.’ Christians have always seen themselves in him. Ask whether you can say it too. And ask which of the two kinds of king you would have chosen that morning: the one with the sword, or the one who would not fight.
